headline: Trump waived the Russia sanctions he signed.
summary: Late Friday night, Trump signed an order waiving the new sanctions on Russia in the Graham Act, a law he signed in September. The act lets the president waive them if he tells Congress it is in the national interest. Senator Thom Tillis, a Republican, called it "beyond irresponsible." It comes a week after his diesel deal with Russia.

cover_question.q: Can a president skip his own law?

cover_answer: This one lets him. Congress wrote the waiver in.
table_question: You make a rule and give yourself an off switch. Is it a rule?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: In September our president signed a rule to punish Russia for its war, and anyone buying Russia's oil. On Friday night he said: not yet. The rule had a pause button written into it, and he pressed it. Grown-ups in Congress are arguing about that, which is their job.
5-7.why: A pause button on a rule. The what, without the why, which the article can't give either.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole event, so the script gives them the pause button and nothing about Putin or the midterms. Vygotsky's point is that the words belong to the adult first, which is why it ends on Congress doing its job. Expect "is Russia the bad guy?" Russia started the war, and that is enough for now.

8-12.script: In September Trump signed a law with heavy penalties for Russia and anyone buying its oil. Congress gave the president a switch to turn them off if he says it is in the national interest. Friday night he flipped it. A referee writes a rule, then waves off the first foul.
8-12.why: Rule, switch, flip. A chain they can follow, and a fairness call to make.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out whether adults apply the rules they announce, so the script runs the chain in order: the law, the switch Congress built into it, the flip. The referee makes the fairness question theirs. Expect "is that allowed?" Yes, the law says so. Then "is it fair?" Senators in both parties say no.

13-17.script: If Congress hands the president a switch to turn off its own rule, who decided? Trump signed the Graham Act in September and waived its Russia sanctions Friday night. Second: Tillis, a Republican, called it "beyond irresponsible." What is a chorus worth if it stays a chorus?
13-17.why: Legal switch, loud critics. They can hold both, then ask what comes next.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things: the waiver is legal because Congress wrote it in, and senators from both parties say it is wrong. Kuhn's point is that argument is practised against someone honest, so the script asks what a chorus is worth, not whether Trump is right. Expect "so what happens now?" The article doesn't say.

5-7.a: It started a war on its neighbor, Ukraine. The rule was meant to make that cost Russia money.

8-12.a: Yes. The law lets him waive the sanctions if he tells Congress why. He did.

8-12.q: Why would he let Russia off?
8-12.a: He said "national interests," no more. Critics say he's going easy on Putin.

13-17.q: Can a president skip his own law?
13-17.a: This one lets him. Congress wrote a waiver into the act, and he used it.

13-17.q: Why is a Republican attacking Trump?
13-17.a: Voters see Russia as an enemy, Axios says. Midterms are weeks away.
